videos.title: Waifus incoming, GPT 6 Sol, Grok 4.7, Opus 5.5, Mimo 2.6, Step 5, OpenMuse: AI NEWS
videos.ai_tech_id: Multi-model AI news roundup: GPT-6 Sol/Luna (OpenAI), Grok 4.7 (xAI), Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), Gemini 3.8 TTS (Google), Mimo V2.6 (Xiaomi), Step 5 (StepFun), and OpenMuse (CopilotKit), among other new model and tool releases
summary: theAIsearch runs its regular sponsor-backed weekly AI news roundup, opening with a string of new generative media tools — WorldCrafter, Ming Image, Mira Scene, and Flux 3 Action — before moving into the week's headline model releases.

The core of the video is a rapid-fire tour through major model launches: Google's Gemini 3.8 text-to-speech model, Xiaomi's Mimo V2.6, StepFun's Step 5, xAI's Grok 4.7, OpenAI's newly introduced GPT-6 Sol and its companion Luna model, and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, alongside a mention of Anthropic's research on using Claude to help discover a novel enzyme system.

It closes on what the host flags as "the most important part" — coverage of Skild AI's physical self-play soccer robotics work, the OpenMuse and CLM open-source model/tool releases, Aikido's open-weight AI security tooling, and Google's Project Suncatcher — framing the episode as a single digest for keeping up with an unusually dense week of AI announcements.

videos.title: Ask Claude to ask YOU. The secret to better AI prompts?
videos.ai_tech_id: Claude (Anthropic) — a "context interview" prompting technique for surfacing missing background information
summary: Futurepedia shares a short practical tip built around Claude: rather than guessing which background details the model needs to give a good answer, the presenter flips the interaction and has Claude interview the user for the context it's missing.

The recommended workflow is simple — dump in whatever context is on hand even if it's messy and unorganized, and if you're unsure what's relevant, explicitly ask Claude to ask you the clarifying questions it needs before it starts answering.

The video's closing tip is to push back on Claude's first answer rather than accepting it outright, since the model's initial response after the context interview is rarely its best one; the whole approach is pitched as a way to get sharper Claude responses without learning formal prompt-engineering syntax.

videos.title: Meta Muse AI: 3 Ways to Use Its New Agent
videos.ai_tech_id: Meta Muse (Meta) — a new AI agent for Facebook Marketplace and Facebook Groups
summary: Sabrina Ramonov introduces Muse, Meta's new AI agent built to handle tasks across Facebook Marketplace and Facebook Groups, and cautions that several unrelated apps share the Muse name so users need to confirm they're installing Meta's own app.

She walks through three concrete uses: telling Muse the style of item you're shopping for (e.g. a dining table) so it checks Marketplace for matching deals throughout the day instead of you refreshing listings manually; handing Muse photos of items to sell so it drafts the listing and benchmarks pricing against comparable items; and pointing Muse at specific Facebook Groups and a neighborhood service need so it alerts you when a relevant post appears.

Each example follows the same pattern — turning a recurring manual search or listing chore into one delegated task where the user supplies the item, photos, or groups up front and then just reviews what Muse finds or produces.

videos.title: Muse AI Privacy Warning: A User Says It Read His Messages
videos.ai_tech_id: Meta Muse (Meta) — AI agent privacy and permissions concerns
summary: Sabrina Ramonov covers a reported privacy incident involving Meta's Muse AI agent, relaying an account in which Muse allegedly inserted a suggestion into a private message conversation that referenced what the two people were discussing.

According to the account described, the user says he never granted Muse permission to read those messages and that it also lacked calendar access or other personal-data permissions; when he raised the issue with Meta, the video says the company placed the blame on the user, even though his settings screenshots showed the relevant permissions turned off.

The video is careful to note it hasn't independently verified what Muse actually accessed or why it responded that way, and frames the real takeaway as a practical caution: since Facebook and Instagram users already share substantial data with Meta, people testing a new AI agent like Muse should stay alert to whether its behavior actually matches the permissions they believe they've granted.

videos.title: How I Built a $1M Solo AI Business ($0 to $1M)
videos.ai_tech_id: AI-powered content distribution (Blotato.com) and earlier natural-language-processing/speech-recognition AI (Qurious, acquired by Pegasystems)
summary: Sabrina Ramonov narrates her path from a computer-science and physics graduate with $250k in student debt to founding Qurious, an NLP-based healthcare AI startup that pivoted into real-time, AI-driven call guidance for sales and support teams combining streaming speech recognition with natural language processing.

She recounts selling Qurious to Pegasystems in a cash-and-stock deal worth over $10 million, after which the technology was integrated into Pega Voice AI and rolled out to thousands of support agents, before she stepped back to recover from burnout and later pivoted to building an audience by teaching AI to a general audience.

The video centers on her current venture, Blotato.com, an AI-assisted content-distribution SaaS she built solo that now helps thousands of creators and entrepreneurs publish across platforms faster, framed as the culmination of a no-budget, no-team growth story that took her follower count from zero to over 500,000 in six months.
